complexity_detail.description: Lambda expression `Identifier -> Expression`, with the parameter type inferred.

A lambda has no type of its own: it is congruent with the function type of its TARGET TYPE, which the assignment context supplies, and that is what gives `a` its type. The same written lambda means different things in different contexts.

A local variable used but not declared in a lambda body must be final or effectively final, and is captured by value. Tagged static_only for the acceptance half (methodology 04 2.4.1); the capture semantics are what a reader needs to predict aliasing_writable_aliasing.

Evaluating a lambda expression produces a reference to an instance of a class implementing the target interface, but a new object need not be allocated on every evaluation and the identity of the result is not committed.
Method reference expression `Type::method`, here producing the unboxing adapter.
Method invocation expression, used in a chain.
Array type `int[]` and array access `ys[0]`, with its run-time bounds check.
Integer subtraction wraps modulo 2^32; the built-in integer operators do not indicate overflow in any way.

A type argument must be a reference type, so a sequence of ints is a List<Integer> and reaching a primitive stream needs an explicit unboxing step - the reason `Integer::intValue` is in the fragment at all.
Generic method type inference over the chained invocations, which is what gives `xs.stream()` the type Stream<Integer> and makes `mapToInt(Integer::intValue)` applicable.
Collection#stream() returns a sequential Stream with this collection as its source - the clause establishing that the elements are traversed, not copied.
Stream#mapToInt(ToIntFunction) returns an IntStream consisting of the results of applying the given function to the elements of this stream - an intermediate operation.
Intermediate operations are always lazy: traversal does not begin until the terminal operation is executed, so `neg` is applied at toArray() and not where it is passed.
